basic_info: Timing (시간대·타이밍) means sequencing the course so each place is visited at its optimal moment — catching the golden-hour/sunset at a scenic spot, hitting restaurants inside comfortable meal windows before hunger sours the mood, and steering around peak-crowd hours at popular venues. Unlike '활동의 다양성·완급' (activity diversity and pacing), which governs the *internal* contrast and tempo between activity blocks, this factor optimizes each block against *external* clocks: the sun, biological hunger rhythms, and crowd-density cycles. Good timing makes the same list of places feel dramatically better simply by reordering when you arrive at each.
psychology: Several mechanisms make timing consequential. (1) Golden hour / lighting: warm, soft, low-angle light around sunset is flattering (softens skin tones, reduces harsh shadows) and reliably evokes calm, nostalgic, romantic, cinematic feeling, making the moment more memorable and the partner more attractive — a visual-affect effect exploited across photography and film. (2) Hunger and mood ('hangry'): dropping blood glucose impairs emotional regulation and cognition and elevates cortisol/adrenaline and ghrelin, increasing irritability, impulsivity, and risk-taking; the classic Danziger, Levav & Avnaim-Pesso (2011) parole-board finding (favorable rulings ~65% right after a food break vs. ~near zero before) illustrates how badly-timed hunger degrades judgment and generosity — directly relevant to keeping a date pleasant. (3) Crowding and density stress: high density triggers a fight-or-flight stress response (raised heart rate, shallow breathing), causes social withdrawal (less eye contact, less conversation, emotional pulling-away), and produces cognitive/sensory overload that impairs concentration and connection; perceived control buffers this, so avoiding uncontrollable crowds protects conversation quality. (4) Peak-end rule (Kahneman & Fredrickson, 1993): placing the sensory peak (a sunset view, a great meal) deliberately in the sequence and ending on a warm note shapes the remembered evaluation of the whole date. Together these argue for ordering places by their best time-window rather than by mere geography.
how_to_apply: 1) Anchor the course to the day's fixed astronomical events first: look up the sunset time and plan to be at the most scenic/open-view spot (rooftop, riverside, hilltop, beach) about 30-40 minutes before sunset so you catch golden hour and dusk, then build the rest of the course backward and forward from that anchor. 2) Protect meal windows: schedule a real meal before either partner gets hungry (roughly a normal lunch/dinner window), and add a light snack/cafe buffer if a big active block or a long gap would otherwise push eating too late — never let a hungry hour sit between two demanding activities. 3) Dodge crowd peaks: hit popular restaurants slightly before the rush (e.g., early dinner) or reserve; visit high-traffic attractions/markets at off-peak times (weekday, early morning, or later evening) and save weekends/midday for lower-density spots. 4) Reserve or check wait times so queueing doesn't create a hungry, stressed, crowded low point. 5) Order the whole sequence by each venue's best window (e.g., indoor/quiet activity during midday crowd peak -> meal just before dinner rush -> scenic spot at golden hour -> relaxed night cap) rather than by shortest walking distance. 6) Leave slack between blocks so running slightly late doesn't cause you to miss the sunset or hit a crowd surge. 7) End at a time and place that closes the night calmly and warmly for a strong peak-end memory.
common_mistakes: Ignoring sunset time and arriving at the best view after dark or during flat midday light, wasting the most romantic window. Scheduling the meal too late so hunger-driven irritability ('hangry') poisons the mood before food arrives. Booking a famous restaurant or attraction at its absolute peak hour and spending the date in a long queue or a loud, packed room where conversation dies. Optimizing purely for geographic convenience (shortest route) while sending each place to the wrong time slot. Overstuffing the schedule so any delay collapses the whole timing (missed sunset, pushed-back dinner). Treating every venue as time-neutral and not checking day-of-week/holiday crowd patterns, weather, or closing times. Ending the date at an awkward, rushed, or draining moment instead of a calm high note.
examples: 1) Sunset-anchored evening: quiet indoor activity (gallery/bookstore-cafe) during the crowded midday -> early dinner reservation just before the dinner rush (well-fed, relaxed room) -> arrive at a riverside/rooftop viewpoint ~30 min before sunset for golden hour -> a calm night-cap bar to close warmly. The scenic peak lands exactly at the best light and the couple is never hungry or stuck in a crowd. 2) Weekend crowd-avoidance: go to a popular market/attraction early morning when it is empty and pleasant -> brunch before the noon rush -> a relaxed park walk in the afternoon as downtown fills up -> leave the busy area before the evening surge. 3) Snack-buffer fix: an active afternoon (bike ride, hike) with a planned light snack midway so blood sugar stays stable, then a proper dinner timed for right after, avoiding a hangry gap. In each, ordering by optimal time-window — not distance — is what makes the course work.
evidence: Psychological basis: (1) Golden-hour lighting and romantic/flattering affect — https://www.bergreenphotography.com/golden-hour-in-photography-and-why-it-matters-for-sunset-wedding-photos/ ; https://therelationshippsychics.com/love/sunset-meaning-in-relationship/ . (2) Hunger, mood and decision-making ('hangry'), incl. the parole-board finding — https://ticcenter.org/hunger-and-decision-making-the-surprising-brain-connection/ ; hunger/satiety and mood — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7667273/ . (3) Crowding, stress, social withdrawal and perceived control — https://psychology.town/environmental/understanding-crowding-psychological-social-dynamics/ ; Crowding and stress review (Springer) — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02684491 . (4) Peak-end rule (Kahneman & Fredrickson, 1993) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak%E2%80%93end_rule ; https://www.nngroup.com/articles/peak-end-rule/ . Note: the specific '~65% vs. near-zero' parole figures originate from Danziger, Levav & Avnaim-Pesso (2011, PNAS); cited here via secondary summary.
